newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: LME zinc seen powering to fresh peak over US$1,700.
newsitem.headline: LME zinc seen powering to fresh peak over US$1,700.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) zinc prices are seen hitting a new seven-year peak above US$1,700 a tonne later on Tuesday as the focus on Chinese short positions is likely to keep the rally intact, dealers said.

"With the market so focused on China's short positions, there's a lot of fund buying going into the market. Zinc is very strong. There's a general feeling that it will try $1,700," a dealer told Reuters.
A Japanese dealer said there are no signs the zinc rally will ease off soon even though the metal is heavily overbought.
"From the looks of it, it's going to eventually try for $1,800 later in the week," he said.

LME broker Rudolf Wolff said in its daily review that the market is full of talk about the short positions of Chinese smelters and that while "zinc is looking technically overbought...there are no signals to suggest that the rally is over as we continue to target $1,700."

"The Chinese are still seen by the trade as very much short," one dealer said when asked about the Chinese claim on Monday that between half to two-thirds of the estimated 90,000 tonnes of short zinc positions by Zhuzhou smelter on the LME
have been covered.
"I think we'll still see more buying in zinc this afternoon," another dealer said.
An official with the China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC) said on Monday Chinese zinc smelters are short by up to 250,000 tonnes of the metal.

Three-month zinc was quoted by one metal house at 0300 GMT at around $1,670/75 a tonne, up from the late quote on the LME of $1,669/72 a tonne. One dealer said he heard cash zinc being quoted in Singapore at around $1,760 a tonne.
Traders said producers were surprised at the speed of zinc's rise in the market, but added the metal's fundamentals towards the last quarter of the year would support its high price.
LME zinc stocks have dropped to below 400,000 tonnes worldwide and demand is seen rising strongly in 1998, they said.
"It would be healthy for the market to have a correction. But we still see a trend upwards for zinc. Stocks are going down and demand is looking strong, especially for next year," one dealer said.
Elsewhere in the markets, Asian traders expect prices of copper and other base metals to take their cue from zinc.
"That's totally strange, copper following zinc's lead. But copper should just maintain its pattern near these levels," a dealer said.
Rudolf Wolff said, however, that the red metal's close on the lows "does not bode well and is suggestive of further weakness, with tests of support down to $2,340 (a tonne)."
Three-month LME copper was indicated late on Monday at $2,342/45 a tonne.
Physical base metal business in Asia was quiet, with the strong rally on the LME driving consumers to the sidelines.
"The buyers are holding back because of the high prices on the LME. These high prices are making consumers very, very uncomfortable," one trader said.
-- Rene Pastor, Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
